2.title: Why is sleep care hitting a bottleneck?
detailed: So, why is sleep care hitting a bottleneck?
First, it's just one night. That's all the data we get.
Second, it ties up the hospital. It uses a lot of resources and beds.
Third, it's hard on patients. They have to come in just for the test.
And finally, there are blind spots at home. We can't easily tell if treatment is used, or if it works.

3.title: How do today's tests compare?
detailed: PSG covers all sleep diseases, but it needs 20 or more wires, and patients wait 1 to 2 months.
Home sleep testing uses 3 wires. An oximeter or an ECG patch can record for 7 to 14 days.
But they are all uncomfortable, and the patch can cause allergy.
So we need to move past wearable sensors, to monitoring with nothing to wear, night after night.

5.title: Radar principle diagram
detailed: Here is how the radar works.
The radar sends a signal from Tx, and picks up the reflection at Rx.
When the chest moves a little, the received signal changes, in its time of flight, or ToF, and its phase.
From the changes, we rebuild the breathing signal, with no wires.

7.title: Our three published studies: sleep lab, home, and heart
detailed: Our team has three published studies: in the sleep lab, at home, and on the heart.
How it works: a 24-GHz continuous-wave radar, plus deep neural decision trees.
In Study 1, in the sleep lab, we compared the radar side by side with PSG in 196 patients, and got a strong correlation, r = 0.91.
In Study 2, we tested 80 patients at home, for 147 nights, with no professional needed to set it up.
In Study 3, with 72 patients, when the radar picked up periodic breathing, it was linked to lower LVEF.

detailed: So how does it see breathing? The radar turns tiny chest movements into breathing signals.
At the top, normal breathing gives a steady, regular wave.
At the bottom is a respiratory event. During the apnea episode, the wave gets very small, and then breathing comes back.

10.title: Sleep tests watch airflow. Radar watches the chest.
detailed: Sleep tests watch airflow. Radar watches the chest.
In standard scoring, airflow stops, or gets shallow. We only see these events when we measure airflow.
Radar senses the chest rising and falling, not airflow. So if we read chest motion as airflow, we get blind spots.
In an obstructive event, the patient keeps trying to breathe, but no air flows. So chest motion isn't the same as airflow.
That's why the radar has to spot a typical pattern of chest-motion changes.
concise: Sleep tests watch airflow: it stops, or gets shallow. Radar watches the chest.
Radar senses the chest rising and falling, not airflow.
In an obstructive event the chest still moves, so the radar has to spot a typical pattern of chest-motion changes.

11.title: How radar sees a sleep-breathing event
detailed: How does radar see a sleep-breathing event? In five steps of chest-wall motion.
First, normal breathing: the chest moves regularly.
Then apnea onset: the movement drops sharply, or stops.
Then struggling effort: the airway is still closed, so the chest makes small moves.
Then a recovery surge: the airway opens, with one big breath.
And then it goes back to normal.
This whole sequence is the event that radar can detect.
concise: Here is how radar sees a sleep-breathing event, in five steps.
Normal breathing, apnea onset, struggling effort, recovery surge, and back to normal.

13.title: Study 1: How accurate is it in the hospital?
detailed: Study 1: how accurate is it in the hospital?
The radar's bRDI and the AHI from PSG line up well, with r = 0.91, and p < 0.01.
For moderate-to-severe OSA, the accuracy was 90.3%, with a cut-off of 19.2 events/h.
For severe OSA, the accuracy was 92.4%, with a cut-off of 28.86 events/h.
And for multi-class prediction, the average accuracy was 83.7%.

14.title: From research to the ward: a zero-contact care platform
detailed: From research to the ward: this is our zero-contact care platform. We now use the radar every day for our inpatients.
It monitors breathing nonstop, with no contact, and it reads heart rate and bed status from the same radar signal.
If a patient is out of bed too long, or vital signs are abnormal, staff get alerts on the dashboard and LINE Notify.
It received the 2021 SNQ, and the 2022 NHQA, Distinctive Center for our Sleep Center.

19.title: Study 2: Taking it home
detailed: This brings us to Study 2: taking it home.
At home, nothing is controlled: different sleep positions, thick blankets, noise, and no technician.
We had 80 subjects and 147 nights of home sleep, with no staff on site.
We compared the radar with home sleep apnea testing, or HSAT.
Real homes are messy, so we need robust signal processing.
concise: At home, nothing is controlled, and there's no technician.

29.title: Study 3: Can breathing tell us about the heart?
detailed: Now, Study 3: can breathing tell us about the heart?
This study had 72 patients, and it was published by our team in 2025.
Here's what we found. When the radar picks up abnormal breathing, especially periodic breathing, or Cheyne-Stokes, it's linked to a lower LVEF.
Just to be clear: this is an early-warning idea for heart failure, based on associations.
It isn't validated yet for diagnosis or prediction.

30.title: Why does a weaker heart change breathing during sleep?
detailed: Why does a weaker heart change breathing during sleep?

Periodic breathing is associated with impaired cardiac function.
Our radar does not measure CO2. It only sees the breathing pattern.

31.title: Periodic-breathing features & cycle length
detailed: We can measure periodic breathing by features like the cycle length and the hyperpnea length.
When cycle length was measured by CPAP, it was 11x in acute heart failure, 8x in chronic heart failure, and 1x in a normal heart.
And by LVEF, the cycle length goes from 49.1 seconds when LVEF is above 50, up to 85.7 seconds when LVEF is below 20.

37.title: What to take home
detailed: So, what should you take home?
First, it's contactless. A 24-GHz radar can monitor breathing night after night, with nothing to wear.
Second, it's consistent with standard tests: r = 0.91 in the hospital, and r = 0.87 at home.
Third, it's a TFDA-cleared screen for suspected severe OSA, with 90.5% sensitivity.
Fourth, we found associations between periodic breathing and cardiac impairment. So it may help us watch the heart, too.
And finally, our work received national quality awards: SNQ and NHQA.
